content: Physical therapy is a healthcare profession dedicated to the prevention, treatment, and management of movement disorders caused by various conditions and diseases across the lifespan. Physical therapy is administered by licensed physical therapists (PTs) or physical therapist assistants (PTAs) under the supervision of PTs. Other healthcare professionals, such as chiropractors and doctors of osteopathy, may also use physical therapy modalities in their practice. Physical therapy programs often involve the participation of a patient’s caregivers to ensure comprehensive care. A physical therapist evaluates, treats, advises, and educates individuals with movement dysfunctions, physical impairments, pain, or disabilities resulting from trauma, disease, or other conditions. They employ physical agents such as therapeutic exercises, mobilization, manipulation, hydrotherapy, mechanical therapy, and electrotherapy. PTs rely on a patient’s medical history and physical examination to diagnose and develop treatment plans. When necessary, they incorporate laboratory and imaging results, such as X-rays, MRIs, or electromyograms, to refine their approach. Physical therapists work in diverse settings, including outpatient clinics, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, extended care facilities, patient homes, schools, research centers, fitness centers, and sports training facilities. Historically, physical therapy has faced criticism for its limited research foundation, with many practitioners relying on anecdotal evidence. However, organizations like the World Confederation for Physical Therapy and the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) have emphasized the importance of evidence-based practices grounded in scientific research. The origins of physical therapy as a professional discipline date back to 1894, when four nurses in England established the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy. Formal training programs soon followed in other countries, such as the School of Physiotherapy at the University of Otago in New Zealand in 1913 and Reed College in the United States in 1914. Research played a pivotal role in advancing the field, with the first physical therapy research published in the United States in 1921. Mary McMillan founded the Physical Therapy Association (now APTA) in the same year. The field gained further recognition in 1924 when the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation promoted physical therapy as a treatment for polio. In the 1940s, physical therapy treatments primarily consisted of exercises, massage, and traction. By the 1950s, manipulative techniques for the spine and extremity joints became more common, particularly in British Commonwealth countries. The 1970s saw the establishment of the Orthopaedic Section of the APTA and the International Federation of Orthopaedic Manipulative Therapy, which advanced manual therapy globally. The 1980s brought technological advancements, such as computer-assisted rehabilitation, further enhancing the field. Physical therapy modalities include a wide range of techniques and tools. These include active and passive exercises, aerobic and cardiovascular exercises, strengthening and stretching exercises, hydrotherapy, mobilization, manipulation, and various electrical modalities. Electrical modalities include ultrasonic therapy, laser therapy, microwave diathermy, interferential therapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), and shock wave therapy. Each modality has specific indications and contraindications, tailored to the patient’s condition and therapeutic goals. For example, active exercises involve voluntary muscle contractions, while passive exercises rely on external forces to move a body part. Aerobic exercises improve cardiovascular health by increasing oxygen consumption, while strengthening exercises target weakened muscles. Techniques like McKenzie exercises are used for conditions such as low back pain and sciatica, focusing on specific lumbar spine movements. Pelvic floor exercises, such as Kegel exercises, strengthen the pelvic muscles and address urinary incontinence. Electrotherapy involves the therapeutic application of electrical currents to manage pain, stimulate muscles, and promote healing. Modalities like TENS provide non-invasive, drug-free pain relief, while interferential therapy uses medium-frequency currents to achieve low-frequency effects for pain relief and muscle stimulation. Laser therapy, which uses focused light energy, is effective for soft tissue injuries, pain management, and wound healing. Shock wave therapy, characterized by high-pressure waves, is used for conditions like plantar fasciitis, calcaneal spurs, and tendinitis. Physical therapy encompasses several specialty areas, reflecting the diverse needs of patients. Cardiopulmonary physical therapy focuses on patients with cardiovascular and pulmonary disorders, aiming to improve endurance and functional independence. Geriatric physical therapy addresses age-related conditions such as arthritis, osteoporosis, and balance disorders, helping older adults restore mobility and reduce pain. Neurological physical therapy targets individuals with neurological disorders like stroke, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis, working to improve balance, mobility, and functional independence. Orthopedic physical therapy specializes in musculoskeletal conditions, including post-operative rehabilitation, sports injuries, and arthritis. Therapists in this field often use modalities like cryotherapy, iontophoresis, and electrotherapy to expedite recovery. Pediatric physical therapy focuses on infants, children, and adolescents with developmental, neuromuscular, or skeletal disorders, aiming to enhance motor skills, strength, and sensory integration. To practice, physical therapists must graduate from an accredited program and pass the National Physical Therapy Examination. Most programs now offer a Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) degree. Licensure is regulated at the state level, and therapists must meet specific requirements to practice in their respective states. Evidence-based practice is increasingly emphasized in physical therapy, with organizations advocating for the integration of scientific research into clinical decision-making. Despite historical reliance on anecdotal evidence, the profession is moving toward a more research-driven approach. Studies have shown that physical therapists can provide comparable or superior outcomes to orthopedic physicians in certain cases, often at lower costs. Physical therapists have access to a wide range of journals and publications, enabling them to stay informed about advancements in the field. Patient satisfaction with physical therapy is generally high, often attributed to the interpersonal skills of therapists and the quality of care provided.
